sections.title: Warm-up
sections.prompt: Read these aloud before you begin. You do not need to understand every word yet — listen for the German sounds.
sections.lede: Two minutes of speaking warms up the sounds you are about to learn.

sections.title: Learning objectives
sections.lede: By the end of this lesson you will be able to do these things.

sections.title: The big picture
sections.lede: German uses the same Latin alphabet as English, with four extra letters and some very different sound habits.

blocks.text: The German alphabet has 26 basic letters, plus the three umlauts ä, ö and ü and the special letter ß (Eszett). Once you know the letter names and the main sound patterns, you can spell your name, read addresses and ask someone to repeat a word.

items: Most consonants sound close to English, but German is more consistent: a written letter is usually pronounced the same way every time.
The umlauts change the vowel sound: a → ä, o → ö, u → ü.
ß is pronounced like a sharp s. It appears after long vowels and never at the start of a word.
German nouns are always written with a capital letter.

blocks.title: Good news for English speakers
blocks.text: You already know most of the letter shapes. The work is in the sounds, not in learning a new script.

sections.title: Rules & patterns
sections.lede: These four sound patterns unlock most German words you will meet at A1.

rows: soft, breathy; no exact English match

items: Say ei as one glide: e → i. Do not say the English letter name “E-I”.
Say ie as a long ee. The e is silent.
For ch, start an English “y” sound and let air pass; after a, o and u it is rougher, as in Bach.
German z always carries a t: Zeit sounds like “tsait”.

blocks.title: Letter names you will need
blocks.text: When spelling aloud, Germans say “Ah, Beh, Ceh, Deh, Eh, Eff, Geh, Ha, Ih, Jott, Ka, Ell, Emm, Enn, Oh, Peh, Qu, Err, Ess, Teh, Uh, Vau, Weh, Ix, Ypsilon, Zett”.

sections.title: Vocabulary
sections.lede: Listen to each word, then repeat it. The article tells you the noun's gender.

items.example: Der Buchstabe B kommt nach A.
items.exampleEn: The letter B comes after A.

items.example: Ä, ö und ü sind Umlaute.
items.exampleEn: Ä, ö and ü are umlauts.

sections.title: Example sentences
sections.lede: Read each sentence aloud. Notice the capital letter on every noun.

items.en: How do you spell your name?
items.note: buchstabiert is the formal and general “one spells” form.

items.de: Mein Name ist Müller: M, Ü, L, L, E, R.
items.en: My name is Müller: M, U-umlaut, L, L, E, R.
items.note: Germans often name the umlaut rather than saying the plain letter.
Sprichst begins with sch + p; say “shpr-”.

sections.title: Pronunciation
sections.lede: These four sounds separate a clear German accent from an English one.

items.hint: Softer than “ick”. Let air escape between tongue and palate; do not press the tongue hard.
Rougher ch after a, o or u. Think of clearing condensation from a window.
Start with a clean “sh”, then “oo-luh”. No hard k.
Say “ts” as one sound, then “ait”. Never an English z.
Round your lips for “oo”, then try to say “ee” without moving them.

blocks.text: In 1996 a spelling reform reduced the number of ß spellings, but the letter remains in words such as Straße, heißen and groß. Switzerland and Liechtenstein do not use ß at all; they write Strasse and heissen.
If your keyboard has no ß, writing ss is usually understood, but official German texts expect ß after a long vowel.

sections.title: Grammar spotlight
sections.heading: Capital letters: nouns are always capitalised
sections.lede: German capitalises more than English, but the rule is simple and regular.

items: Every noun is capitalised, wherever it appears: das Haus, in der Schule, mit meiner Familie.
The first word of every sentence is capitalised, as in English.
The polite pronoun Sie is capitalised, but the informal du is not.
Adjectives, verbs and adverbs stay lowercase unless they begin a sentence.

rows: Mann is a noun → capital M.
Idee is a noun; gute is an adjective.
du is a pronoun, not a noun.

blocks.title: Exam habit
blocks.text: When you write German, check every noun for a capital letter. Missing noun capitals is one of the most common A1 writing errors.

sections.title: Choose the right answer
sections.lede: Check your understanding of the alphabet, sounds and capitalisation.

exercises.prompt: Which word contains the sound “sh” at the beginning?
exercises.explanation: sch is pronounced “sh”. Schule begins with this sound.

exercises.prompt: How is the letter ß pronounced?
exercises.explanation: ß is a sharp s, as in Straße.
The sentence starts with a capital letter and Hund is a noun, so it also takes a capital. Hund is masculine, so ein becomes einen in the accusative.

exercises.prompt: Which letter combination sounds like English “ee”?
exercises.explanation: ie is a long ee sound, as in wie. ei sounds like “eye”.

exercises.prompt: What does “Wie buchstabiert man das?” mean?
exercises.explanation: buchstabieren means to spell, so the question asks how something is spelled.

sections.title: Complete the sentence
sections.lede: Type the missing word. Pay attention to capitals.

exercises.explanation: das Alphabet = the alphabet. Nouns take a capital letter.
The letter ß is called das Eszett.
die Sprache = language. It is a noun, so it is capitalised.

sections.title: Build the sentence
sections.lede: Click the words in the correct order, then check your sentence.

exercises.prompt: Build: “How do you spell your name?”
exercises.explanation: A W-question starts with the question word, then the verb: Wie buchstabiert man …?
Mein Name ist … is the standard way to give your name.
Yes/no questions start with the verb: Sprichst du …?

sections.lede: Listen to the dialogue twice. Then answer without reading the transcript.

script.en: S, C, H, R, O-umlaut, D, E, R.

sections.title: Speaking
sections.lede: Say your own name and spell it aloud. Repeat until the letter names feel automatic.
sections.prompt: Introduce yourself and spell your first name letter by letter.

model.de: Guten Tag. Ich heiße Alex. A, L, E, X.
model.en: Good day. My name is Alex. A, L, E, X.

tips: Say the German letter names, not the English ones: Ah, Beh, Ceh, Deh …
If your name contains an umlaut, say the letter name and add “Umlaut”: Ü = “U-Umlaut”.
Record yourself, then compare your pace with the model. Clarity matters more than speed.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.lede: These errors are normal at the start. Notice the pattern behind each correction.

items.why: Names take a capital letter, and German nouns are always capitalised.
The verb must agree with du: buchstabieren → buchstabierst.
Countries are nouns and are capitalised in German.
ß is always a sharp s, never voiced like English z.

sections.title: Lesson assessment
sections.lede: Ten questions. Score 70% or more to unlock the next lesson. You can retake this check as often as you need.

questions.prompt: Which letter combination is pronounced like English “eye”?
questions.explanation: ei sounds like “eye”, as in mein. ie sounds like “ee”.

questions.prompt: How many umlauts does German have?
questions.explanation: The umlauts are ä, ö and ü — three in total.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?
questions.explanation: The sentence starts with a capital, and Mann is a noun, so both are capitalised.

questions.prompt: What is the German name for the letter ß?
Which word begins with the “ts” sound?
questions.explanation: German z is pronounced “ts”, so Zeit begins with a ts sound.
man buchstabiert = one spells. The verb ends in -t with man.
Countries are nouns and take a capital letter: Indien.
Mein Name ist … is the standard introduction pattern.
Question word + verb + subject: Wie buchstabiert man das?
